In Short
  • What I Owned: The concept, the core systems (cards, economy, mana, combat), all 40+ cards and the board, and the backlog and roadmap for a 15-person team.
  • Hardest Problem: Fog of War, it came difficult to balance the rule of the fog of war with the amount of different behavior from the cards.
  • What it Shows: Leading a project from idea to release, and an economy built to force a real choice every turn.

1. Every turn is a trade-off. One resource for everything means no free actions.

2. Readable at a glance. Players understand a card's role from its type and layout.

3. Easy to learn, deep to master.

blocks.text: 1. One Pool of Mana for Everything

blocks.html: Many card games give separate resources for different actions. Here, moving, attacking and defending all draw from the same mana pool, so every turn is a trade-off: spending to advance leaves less to protect yourself.

blocks.text: 3. Testing on Paper and in Simulation

blocks.html: I validated the concept with paper prototypes before any engine work, then balanced it with spreadsheets and Machinations simulations of the mana economy, and used playtests to find balance problems the models missed.

• Problem: Players could see everything and planned too far ahead removing the strategy aspect of the game.

• Cause: Having no way to block your vision, the player could create their strategy from turn 1 without hesitations. Player 1 almost had 100% of advantage when starting the game.

• Fix: I designed a fog-of-war feature that hides everything besides the player's terrains and units. Players could gain more vision by placing terrains and units in the board 

• Result: This change made players create a defensive thought before actually taking actions, which reduced players frustrations in 60% and made the game more even.

I led design, art and engineering through close collaboration for the whole project, owned the backlog and roadmap, and set feature priorities. I built spreadsheets that made handoffs between departments faster.

In addition leading the project from the design and project management position, I cut the amount of cards from each deck to ensure it would be delivered for the test. It increased the balancing work although the balancing pipeline was already established which had less effect when it came time to cut down the scope.

What Worked: Simulating the economy before building it.

What I'd do Differently: Create design test pipelines early in the project to ensure tests and failures can be gathered before the actual implementation inside the engine.

What I Learned: A single shared resource creates interesting decisions every turn, but it needs careful simulation to stay balanced; leading a 15-person team showed me that a clear roadmap is a design tool too.
